overview.body:
**Zéphyros** (*zephyros*) — West Wind · The west wind — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "West Wind". The name means "The west wind"[^1].

Zéphyros is the **west wind** of the Greeks — the mildest of the four Anemoi, the breeze that **loosens winter** and calls up the flowers. Where Bóreas rages and Nótos drowns ships in rain, Zéphyros is the wind the poets loved: the steady, **fruit-bearing breath** that fans the orchards of the blessed and carries spring north into the human world.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Zéphyros** and serves its temple at [zéphyros.com](https://xn--zphyros-bya.com). The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *zephyros* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Ζέφυρος**. Etymologically it means "The west wind"[^1].

The ASCII form *zephyros* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Zéphyros** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **z** → **Z** — Z uppercase
- **e** → **é** — Acute on e
- **p** → **p** — p same
- **h** → **h** — h same
- **y** → **y** — y same
- **r** → **r** — r same
- **o** → **o** — o same
- **s** → **s** — s same

The project holds the domain **zéphyros.com** (xn--zphyros-bya.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.
Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈzdɛ.pʰy.ros/** — Attic Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Zé-** — stressed first syllable; classical zeta was a true 'zd' cluster, as in English 'wisdom', not a modern 'z'
- **-phy-** — phi was an aspirated p (p + breath), not an f; upsilon was a rounded French-like 'u' [y]
- **-ros** — short final -os; the r lightly trilled

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'ZDEH-phee-ros' — stress the first syllable; begin with the 'zd' of 'wisdom', and let the phi puff air like an English 'up-hill', not an 'f'

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — ζόφος (zophos), 'gloom, darkness; the dark quarter of the sky — the west' — the word's likely kin, naming the wind from the quarter it blows from
- **PIE** — uncertain; Beekes flags the formation as possibly Pre-Greek rather than securely Indo-European

Tier-2 — Accent-Preserving. The restoration Zéphyros preserves the acute stress of Ζέφυρος on the first syllable, a feature plain ASCII loses; it carries no long-vowel mark, so a single preserved feature places the name in Tier 2.

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

original-script.body: The name is written in Greek as **Ζέφυρος**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *zephyros* and the PuniCodex restoration **Zéphyros** are measured: the restoration preserves its pitch accent of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

symbols.body:
The iconography associated with Zéphyros concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **Garland of Flowers** — On the Tower of the Winds in Athens, Zéphyros is carved as a youth whose folded cloak spills blossoms — his spring-bearing nature made visible in stone.
- **Wings** — Like all the Anemoi, he is winged in Greek and Roman art; the winds fly, and their wings mark them as powers of the air rather than ordinary gods.
- **Swift Horses** — By Pódargē the harpy he fathered Xánthos and Bálios, the immortal horses of Achilles — the wind's own speed given equine form.
- **The Swallow** — The swallow's return was proverbially bound to the west wind's season; both were the first messengers that winter had broken.
- **Billowing Sail** — A kind wind for sailors: steady, mild, and western — the breeze that fills canvas without violence and carries ships home.
- **Youthful Bloom** — In art he appears as a beautiful, unbearded youth, a wind conceived not as a destroyer but as a lover — fitting the bridegroom of Chlōris.

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

mythology.body:
Zéphyros is a minor god with an outsized poetic life: born of Dawn, lover of flowers, father of the fastest horses ever to run. His myths are few but luminous — each one binds the west wind to speed, desire, and the returning spring.[^1]

### Son of Dawn and the Starry Sky (Birth of the Winds)

In *Theogony* 378–380, Hesiod records that Eōs (Dawn) bore to Astraios, the starry dusk, the mighty winds: **Zéphyros**, **Bóreas**, and **Nótos** — 'a goddess lying in love with a god'. The genealogy is exact: the clearing west wind is the child of first light and the star-field, born at the seam where night opens into day.[^2]

### Father of Achilles's Horses (Iliad)

In *Iliad* 16 (149–151), Patroklos harnesses Achilles's immortal pair, Xánthos and Bálios, 'whom Pódargē, the harpy swift of foot, bore to **Zéphyros** the west wind as she grazed in a meadow beside the stream of Ōkeanos'. A wind coupling with a storm-snatcher in a meadow: Homer makes the horses' supernatural speed a literal inheritance. It is Xánthos, this same wind-begotten colt, who later speaks with a human voice to foretell Achilles's death (*Iliad* 19, 404–417).

### The Abduction of Chlōris (Roman Flora)

In Ovid's *Fasti* 5 (195–214), the goddess Flora tells her own story: 'I who am now called Flora was once Chlōris… **Zéphyros** saw me, desired me, and carried me off' — then made her his lawful wife and gave her dominion over every flower, so that in her garden 'it is always spring'. Hyginus (*Fabulae*) preserves the fruit of the union: their son **Karpós**, 'Fruit' itself, the harvest that follows blossom.

### The Breeze of the Blessed Orchards (Odyssey)

In *Odyssey* 7 (112–132), the garden of King Alkinoös on Scheria — fruit upon fruit, pear ripening on pear, never failing winter or summer — is kept in perpetual bearing because 'the **breath of Zéphyros**, ever blowing, causes some fruits to swell and others to ripen'. Homer needs no allegory here: the west wind simply is the climate of paradise, the mildest air imaginable, made divine.

sources.citation: Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.
Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.

syncretism.body:
The Romans called him **Favōnius**, from *favēre*, 'to favor' — the propitious wind — and married him to their own flower-goddess Flōra, whose festival, the Floralia, kept the Greek Chlōris-marriage alive in cult. Horace (*Odes* 1.4) sings winter loosening 'under the welcome west wind', and Virgil lets Favonius breathe through the *Georgics* as the air that unbinds the fields. Through Latin poetry the name passed intact into every European vernacular: the gentle west wind of Greece became the *zephyr* of the modern world.[^1]

Within the Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ananke|Anánkē]].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

cultural-legacy.body: English **zephyr** — 'a soft, gentle breeze' — descends directly from his name through Latin *zephyrus*, and has been a staple of English verse since Chaucer opened the *Canterbury Tales* with 'Zephirus… with his sweete breeth' quickening the spring crops. The word also gave its name to a fine, light yarn and to anything featherweight. Few Greek wind-gods survive so completely: not as a character, but as the very word English reaches for when the air turns kind.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

archaeology.body: Zéphyros's most famous monument is the **Tower of the Winds** (Horologion of Andronikos Kyrrhestēs, 1st c. BCE) in the Roman Agora of Athens, whose octagonal frieze personifies the eight winds — Zéphyros on the west face as a youth scattering flowers from his folded cloak. Pausanias (2.12.1) records a sanctuary with an altar of the Winds at Titanē in Sikyonia, where a priest sacrificed to them annually — one of the few attested cult sites for the Anemoi as a group. In Rome, his cult life ran through his bride: the temple of Flora near the Circus Maximus and the games of the Floralia.[^1]

sources.citation: Pausanias, Description of Greece, Loeb Classical Library, 180.

meditation.body: The Greeks did not usually worship the winds with temples and myths of their own — they felt them, and feeling was enough. Zéphyros is the clearest case of a natural force crossing into personality precisely because it was *pleasant*: the storm winds stay brute daimones, but the wind that opens the flowers earned a wife, a marriage bed, and children. His ambivalence is quiet but real — the same wind that breeds Achilles's immortal horses also breeds the speed that carries the hero toward death. For the Greeks the west wind was proof that the divine could be gentle without ceasing to be power: a daimon you pray to by opening the orchard gate.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

homeric-hymns.body: Of all Zéphyros' absences this is the most telling: no Homeric Hymn to him survives — nor to any wind. The corpus of thirty-three hymns lavishes its long forms on Olympians and its shortest on a few cosmic powers — Helios, Selene, Mother Earth[^1] — yet the Anemoi never win even a closing formula. The silence is diagnostic: hymns track cult and sacrifice, and the winds lived in epic as weather-functions, not recipients of song. What survives is hymnic matter inside narrative verse: Hesiod's catalogue of Eos' children by Astraeus, where Zéphyros is born 'bright-blowing' (ἀργεστής), and the Theogony's exemption of Notos, Boreas and Zéphyros from the Typhon-born blasts — three gods by descent, a blessing to mortals.[^2] In the Iliad the winds are approached liturgically rather than hymned: Achilles vows rich offerings to Boreas and Zéphyros, and Iris finds the Anemoi feasting in Zéphyros' own hall.[^3] Only centuries later does the west wind receive his hymn outright: Orphic Hymn 81 addresses Zéphyros with its prescribed fumigation, late piety granting at last what the classical hymnist withheld.[^4]

sources.citation: Homeric Hymns 31–32 (To Helios, To Selene) — the collection's only hymns to natural powers; no hymn to any wind survives.
Hesiod, Theogony 378–380 (the wind-sons of Eos and Astraeus) and 869–871 (the three 'good' winds).
Homer, Iliad 23.194–213 (Achilles' vow; the winds feasting in the house of Zephyrus).
Orphic Hymn 81, To Zephyrus (Ζεφύρου).

epithets.body:
Zéphyros is nearly bare of cult titles: the Greeks sacrificed to winds collectively, and epic gave him descriptors, not liturgical names. What adheres:

- **ἀργεστής** (*arghestēs*) — 'bright-blowing, sky-clearing'; his one fixed epic epithet, given at his birth in the catalogue of Eos' wind-sons.[^1]
- **Ζεφυρίη** (*Zephyríē*) — 'the Zephyr-breeze'; Homer's feminine by-form for the west air that never ceases over Alcinous' orchards, swelling some fruit, ripening another.[^2]
- **Ζέφυρος** (*Zéphyros*) — 'the Westerner, the one out of the gloaming'; the name derives from ζόφος, the dark quarter where the sun sets — Homer's 'murky ζόφος' — so his very name is a directional title.[^3]
- **πόσις Χλωρίδος** (*pósis Chlōrídos*) — 'husband of Chloris'; not liturgical but the standing relational tag of later tradition, canonized when Ovid's Flora recalls she was Chloris before the wind wed her.[^4]
- **πατὴρ Καρποῦ** (*patèr Karpoû*) — 'father of Carpus (Fruit)'; the late genealogical tag under which Nonnus tells of Carpus and the reed Calamus.[^4]

sources.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 378–380 (ἀργεστὴν Ζέφυρον).
Homer, Odyssey 7.117–119 (the ever-blowing Ζεφυρίη in the gardens of Alcinous).
Homer, Iliad 12.239–240 (ποτὶ ζόφον ἠερόεντα); cf. Chantraine, DELG s.v. ζόφος.

oracle-sites.body:
No oracle of Zéphyros exists, and no sanctuary was ever his alone; his cult life is collective, folded into the Anemoi. The honest record is a tour of shared wind-cults.

- **Tower of the Winds, Athens** — the Horologion of Andronicus Cyrrhestes (c. 100–50 BC), an octagonal marble tower with sundials, a water-clock and a bronze Triton vane, its faces carved with the eight winds — Zéphyros on the west. Not a temple, but antiquity's nearest approach to a civic monument of him.[^1]
- **Altar of the Winds at Titane** — near Sicyon, a priest sacrificed to the winds one night each year, with secret rites at four pits and 'Medea's spells' chanted to tame the blasts.[^2]
- **Delphi and Thyia** — the winds' one oracular link is indirect: the Delphic oracle itself ordered sacrifices to them, and Thyia's altar still received offerings in Herodotus' day; Athens' famous wind-shrine was Boreas', not his.[^3]
- **Cape Zephyrion, Egypt** — the promontory near Canopus bore his name and held the Ptolemaic temple of Arsinoe-Aphrodite Zephyritis; the cult, though, was the queen-goddess's — the wind lent only his toponym.[^4]

sources.citation: Vitruvius, De architectura 1.6.4; cf. Varro, De re rustica 3.5.17 (the Tower of the Winds).
Pausanias, Description of Greece 2.12.1 (the altar of the Winds at Titane).
Herodotus 7.178 (the Delphians' altar to the winds at Thyia); 7.189 (the Athenian shrine of Boreas).
Strabo, Geography 17.1.16 (Cape Zephyrion and the temple of Arsinoe Aphrodite); Callimachus, Epigram 5 Pfeiffer.

iconography.body:
Ancient art knows two Zéphyroi: the winged pursuer of Classical vases and the unwinged, flower-laden youth of the Hellenistic city.

- **Winged youth with Hyakinthos** — on Attic red-figure of the early fifth century BC he flies after the Spartan youth on spread wings, the same winged-pursuer scheme as Boreas chasing Oreithyia; catalogued under 'Hyakinthos' and 'Zephyros'.[^1]
- **Flower-strewer of the Tower of the Winds** — on the tower's west face he walks unwinged, a youth whose gathered chlamys-fold is heaped with the flowers he scatters; standard documentation in Stuart and Revett.[^2]
- **Bearer of Psyche** — Apuleius' Zephyr, wafting Psyche down from the fatal rock, becomes a favourite of Roman painting and gems: the wind as soft carrier of brides.[^3]
- **The puffed-cheek wind-head** — on Roman sarcophagi and floor mosaics the Anemoi shrink to tousled, swollen-cheeked heads at the corners of the design, a generic type into which Zéphyros is folded unnamed.[^4]

His most famous image is post-antique: Botticelli's winged god seizing Chloris in the Primavera (Uffizi) fuses both ancient types into one.
